mcqs.question: In the BankAccount example, what does making `balance` private and only mutating it through `withdraw()`/`deposit()` actually buy you?
options: It makes the class run faster, since private fields skip an access-control check at runtime
It prevents any external code from putting the balance into an invalid state, since only vetted methods can change it
It automatically makes the class thread-safe under concurrent access
It hides the balance field from the compiler, so type errors on it are no longer caught
mcqs.explanation: Private fields plus controlled methods mean only code that enforces the invariant (never negative) can change balance. There's no runtime speed benefit, private fields don't imply thread safety, and the compiler still fully type-checks private fields — it just restricts which code may reference them.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes what encapsulation and abstraction each protect against?
options: Encapsulation prevents callers from touching internal state directly; abstraction prevents callers from needing to understand internal complexity
Encapsulation and abstraction both refer to hiding a class's private fields from other classes
Abstraction is a Java-only concept; encapsulation applies to every OOP language
Encapsulation is achieved only through interfaces; abstraction is achieved only through access modifiers
mcqs.explanation: Encapsulation is about controlling access to state; abstraction is about hiding complexity behind a simple contract. Both concepts exist in every mainstream OOP language, and the mechanisms are swapped in the wrong options — interfaces drive abstraction, access modifiers drive encapsulation.

mcqs.question: Does implementing an interface, by itself, give a class encapsulation?
options: Yes, because an interface enforces private fields on every implementing class
Yes, because interfaces and encapsulation are the same mechanism
No — interfaces provide neither abstraction nor encapsulation, only inheritance
No — the interface gives abstraction (a hidden implementation); encapsulation still depends on the implementing class protecting its own state
mcqs.explanation: An interface has no state of its own to protect, so it can't grant encapsulation — it only defines a contract, which is abstraction. Encapsulation depends entirely on whether the concrete class keeps its fields private and enforces its invariants.

mcqs.question: A candidate says "abstraction and encapsulation are basically the same thing — both just hide stuff." What's the sharpest correction?
options: They're right — for interview purposes the distinction doesn't matter
Encapsulation only applies to functional programming, so the comparison is invalid
Encapsulation hides data behind access control; abstraction hides complexity behind a simple interface — a class can score high on one while scoring low on the other
Abstraction is a compile-time-only concept while encapsulation only exists at runtime, so they can't be compared
mcqs.explanation: The two hide different things and can vary independently in the same class — a getter-heavy class can be fully encapsulated yet leak complexity, or a public struct can hide complexity behind free functions with no encapsulation at all. Neither is compile-time-only or language-restricted.
